{{Short description|Mathematical estimate of inbreeding}}
{{distinguish|Coefficient of relationship}}

The '''coefficient of inbreeding''' ('''COI''') is a number measuring how [[inbreeding|inbred]] an individual is. Specifically, it is the [[probability]] that two [[alleles]] at any [[Locus (genetics)|locus]] in an individual are identical by descent from a [[common ancestor]] of the two parents.<ref name=Wright1922>{{citation
  | title = Coefficients of Inbreeding and Relationship
  | last = Wright
  | first = Sewall
  | journal = The American Naturalist
  | year = 1922
  | volume = 56
  | issue = 645
 | pages = 330–338
  | doi=10.1086/279872|doi-access=free| bibcode = 1922ANat...56..330W
 }}</ref><ref>{{citation
  | last = Redei
  | first = George P.
  | year = 2004
  | title = Encyclopedic Dictionary of Genetics, Genomics and Proteomics
  | publisher = John Wiley and Sons, Inc.}}</ref><ref>{{citation
  | last = Charlesworth
  | first = Deborah
  | title = Inbreeding
  | encyclopedia = Encyclopedia of Life Sciences
  | year = 2005
  | publisher = John Wiley and Sons, Inc.}}</ref><ref>{{citation
  | last1 = Falconer
  | first1 = D.S.
  | last2 = Mackay
  | first2 = T.F.C.
  | year = 1996
  | title = Introduction to Quantitative Genetics
  | edition = 4
  | publisher = Longman}}</ref> A higher COI will make the traits of the offspring more predictable, but also increases the risk of health issues. In dog breeding, it is recommended to keep the COI less than 5%; however, in some breeds this may not be possible without [[outcrossing]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.instituteofcaninebiology.org/blog/coi-faqs-understanding-the-coefficient-of-inbreeding|access-date=Feb 5, 2024|title=COI FAQS: Understanding the Coefficient of Inbreeding|publisher=The Institute of Canine Biology|author=Carol Beuchat|date=June 4, 2015}}</ref> The average COI for dog breeds is 25%.<ref>{{cite journal|title=The effect of inbreeding, body size and morphology on health in dog breeds|publisher=Springer Nature|author=Danika Bannasch|journal=Canine Medicine and Genetics |date=December 2, 2021 |volume=8 |issue=1 |article-number=12 |doi=10.1186/s40575-021-00111-4 |doi-access=free |pmid=34852838 |pmc=8638537 }}</ref>

==Calculation==
An individual is said to be inbred if there is a loop in its [[pedigree chart]]. A loop is defined as a path that runs from an individual up to the [[common ancestor]] through one parent and back down to the other parent, without going through any individual twice. The number of loops is always the number of common ancestors the parents have. If an individual is inbred, the coefficient of inbreeding is calculated by summing all the probabilities that an individual receives the same allele from its father's side and mother's side. As every individual has a 50% chance of passing on an allele to the next generation, the formula depends on 0.5 raised to the power of however many generations separate the individual from the common ancestor of its parents, on both the father's side and mother's side. This number of generations can be calculated by counting how many individuals lie in the loop defined earlier. Thus, the coefficient of inbreeding ''f'' of an individual X can be calculated with the following formula:<ref>Schonewald-Cox, C.M., S.M. Chambers, B. MacBryde, and L. Thomas (eds.). 1983. Genetics and Conservation. Benjamin/Cummings, Menlo Park, Calif.
</ref><ref name=Wright1922/>

<math display="block">f_X = \sum_N 0.5^{n - 1} \cdot (1 + f_A)</math>
where <math>n</math> is the number of individuals in the aforementioned loop, <br><math>N</math> is the number of common ancestors (loops), <br> and <math>f_A</math> is the coefficient of inbreeding of the common ancestor of X's parents.

To give an example, consider the following pedigree.
[[File:Avunculate Mating.svg|thumb|G is the progeny of C and F, and C is the biological uncle of F.]]

In this pedigree chart, G is the progeny of C and F, and C is the biological [[uncle]] of F. To find the coefficient of inbreeding of G, first locate a loop that leads from G to the [[common ancestor]] through one parent and back down to the other parent without going through the same individual twice. There are only two such loops in this chart, as there are only 2 common ancestors of C and F. The loops are G – C – A – D – F and G – C – B – D – F, both of which have 5 members.

Because the common ancestors of the parents (A and B) are not inbred themselves, <math>f_A = 0</math>. Therefore the coefficient of inbreeding of individual G is <math>f_G = (0.5^4 + 0.5^4)\cdot(1+0) = 12.5\%</math>. 

If the parents of an individual are not inbred themselves, the coefficient of inbreeding of the individual is one-half the [[coefficient of relationship]] between the parents. This can be verified in the previous example, as 12.5% is one-half of 25%, the coefficient of relationship between an uncle and a niece.

== Iterated sibling mating ==
One simple special case is starting by mating two unrelated parents ("the founders"), but then in each generation mate two siblings from the previous generation. This case may be analysed directly from the loop summation formula. The offspring of the mating of the founders are not inbred (although they have a positive [[coefficient of relationship]]); therefore, they may be called "generation&nbsp;0". (However, note, that this technically makes the founders to "generation&nbsp;−1".) 

Thus, the inbreeding coefficient <math>f_g</math> equals 0 for <math>g=0</math> (and for <math>g=-1</math>). For any positive integer ''g'', any individual in generation ''g'', and any generation ''h'' earlier than the parents of that individual, there are exactly <math>2^{g-h-1}</math> loops through that individual connecting to an 'earliest common common ancestor' of generation ''h''; and each such loop contains in total <math>2(g-h)-1</math> ancestors. 

The inbreeding coefficient <math>f_g</math> for this individual may be calculated recursively:
::<math>f_g = \sum_{h=-1}^{g-2} 2^{g-h-1} 2^{-(2(g-h)-1)} (1+f_h) = \sum_h 2^{-(g-h)} (1+f_h) = \sum_{i=2}^{g+1} 0.5^i (1+f_{g-i})\,.</math>
(The simplifications employ some [[Exponentiation#Integer exponents|exponentiation rules]], and substituting ''i'' for <math>g-h</math>.) This can be expressed in closed form as
::<math>f_g=\frac{1}{5} 2^{-2 g-1} \left(\left(2 \sqrt{5}-5\right) \left(1-\sqrt{5}\right)^g+5\times\ 2^{2 g+1}-\left(2 \sqrt{5}+5\right) \left(\sqrt{5}+1\right)^g\right).</math>

In other words, we get <math>f_1 = 0.5^2 = 0.25</math>, <math>f_2 = 0.5^2+0.5^3 = 0.375</math>, <math>f_3 = 0.5^2\cdot0.25 + 0.5^3 + 0.5^4 = 0.5</math>, and so on. Expressing the coefficients as rounded percents yields the following table:
